artist: Sam Doores + Riley Downing & The Tumbleweeds
label: Self-released
description: The pre-Deslondes trio's only album, cut by Sam Doores and Riley Downing (later of The Deslondes) with Dan Cutler under the Tumbleweeds name, in the ramshackle country-blues style they'd carry into the Deslondes. It leans on upright bass, loose acoustic guitars, and weathered group harmonies, closer to a porch session than a studio record. It's for anyone tracing the roots of the Deslondes' street-corner sound back before the band had its name.
lineage: Grew directly out of Doores and Downing busking and playing New Orleans dive bars in the early 2010s; the Tumbleweeds renamed themselves The Deslondes in 2013.

label: New West Records
description: Doores' debut solo record, largely written and recorded in Berlin, widens his palette beyond the Deslondes' New Orleans R&B-and-country stew into Tin Pan Alley-style pop, cabaret piano, and wandering acoustic folk. Songs like 'Let It Roll' and 'Other Side of Town' keep his easy, conversational drawl but trade the full band's boogie for a more intimate, ragtime-tinged arrangement. It's for Deslondes fans curious what one member sounds like stripped down and abroad.
lineage: A solo detour from The Deslondes, following his co-founding of Mashed Potato Records and Studio in New Orleans.

label: New West Records
description: Downing's first solo album, produced by Andrija Tokic with fellow Deslonde John James Tourville playing across it, is a leaner, more straightforwardly honky-tonk record than his main band, built on twangy electric guitar, pedal steel, and plainspoken breakup songs. The title track and 'Coleman Rose' lean into a classic country shuffle. It's the record for listeners who want the Deslondes' rootsier, more countrified side isolated and pushed forward.
lineage: A solo record from the Deslondes' co-frontman, keeping the band's New West home and its New Orleans country-band circle intact (Tourville produces and plays).

label: New West Records
description: Made after founding drummer Cameron Snyder left the band, this is a stripped-back, road-worn return to the group's original five-way songwriting swap, described by the band as their rawest and most honest record since their debut. 'Hold on Liza' and 'Pour Another Round' keep the barroom piano and multi-voice harmonies that define the band's sound, with less studio polish than 'Hurry Home' or 'Ways & Means.' It's for longtime fans following the band through a lineup change.
lineage: Fourth Deslondes studio LP; New Orleans Americana quintet continuing the lineage of Doores, Downing, Cutler and Tourville's shared songwriting project.

label: Mashed Potato Records
description: A three-song live-to-tape demo session cut at Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Studio, catching Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's paired voices before they had a full band identity. Doores plays piano and Cameron Snyder drums on the session, tying the duo directly to the Deslondes' orbit. It's a rough-edged curiosity for tracing the Lostines back to their earliest New Orleans sessions.
lineage: Recorded at Mashed Potato Studio with Deslondes members Sam Doores and Cameron Snyder sitting in, the same New Orleans DIY-country scene as the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: The New Orleans duo's proper debut EP, recorded live to tape at Mashed Potato Records, built on the two singers' tightly stacked harmonies over spare guitar and rhythm section. Tracks like 'Faith In Love' and 'Who's Your Love' favor early rock-and-roll and girl-group phrasing filtered through a country-folk band. It's the entry point for the Lostines' pre-full-length sound.
lineage: Grew out of the same Mashed Potato Records/Studio scene as Sam Doores and the Deslondes.

label: Gar Hole Records / Mashed Potato Records
description: A split EP pairing two songs from The Lostines with two from Nick Shoulders & the Okay Crawdad, released jointly by Gar Hole Records and Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records to mark their overlapping years coming up in New Orleans. The Lostines' side moves from the electric-guitar dancehall stomp of 'A Tear' to the string-and-keyboard hush of 'Last Night'. It documents the small-label, shared-scene connections around the New Orleans Americana underground.
lineage: A cross-label collaboration linking The Lostines' Mashed Potato Records roots to Nick Shoulders' Gar Hole Records, both offshoots of the same New Orleans DIY country scene.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: The Lostines' full-length debut folds 1960s girl-group harmony singing into a New Orleans roots-band frame, with Cajun fiddle, pedal steel, baritone guitar, and swooning strings behind Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's tightly entwined voices. Sam Doores co-produced and plays on the record, and songs like 'Neon Lights' and 'Full Moon Night' move between late-night dancehall pop and quieter, string-laced balladry. It's the best entry point to the duo's sound.
lineage: Deepens the Mashed Potato Records/Sam Doores connection first heard on their earlier EPs; part of the same New Orleans Americana community as the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff.

label: Bloodshot Records
description: Winslow-King's Bloodshot Records debut blends New Orleans R&B horns, ragtime-inflected fingerpicking, and slide guitar into a warm, gospel-tinged roots-rock sound. It's brighter and more arranged than straight blues, built around his easy tenor and duets with then-wife Esther Rose. Good for listeners who want the city's brass-band and blues traditions filtered through a songwriter's frame.
lineage: Part of the same early-2010s New Orleans street-and-club folk scene as Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes; Esther Rose sang and played in his band before her solo career.

album: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always
label: Bloodshot Records
description: A sunnier, more electric-leaning follow-up to 'Everlasting Arms', mixing slide-guitar blues, breezy horn charts, and New Orleans second-line rhythm into concise, hook-forward songs. It trades some of the earlier record's gospel weight for a looser, dance-ready feel. It suits listeners drawn to the city's blues-and-brass lineage more than pure country twang.
lineage: Continues Winslow-King's run on Bloodshot Records within the same New Orleans roots-music circle as the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff.

label: Self-released
description: Quintana's debut solo album after years singing traditional jazz in the French Quarter, mixing folk songwriting with the French, Cajun, and R&B threads of her hometown. It's a quieter, singer-songwriter record built around acoustic guitar and her clear alto, closer to porch-folk than her later, more band-driven work. For listeners tracing New Orleans folk voices adjacent to the Riff Raff/Deslondes scene.
lineage: Emerged from the same early-2010s New Orleans street-folk and traditional-jazz crossover scene as Hurray for the Riff Raff.

label: Self-released
description: A concept record built around New Orleans' relationship to the Mississippi River, pairing Quintana's folk guitar and voice with jazz and Cajun-inflected arrangements. It's more fleshed-out than her debut, with a full band supporting a set of story-songs about place and water. Good for fans of literate, regionally rooted folk songwriting.
lineage: Follows Quintana's shift from traditional jazz sideman work into solo songwriting within the New Orleans Americana scene.

label: Self-released
description: A short, intimate EP of acoustic story-songs, smaller in scale than her full-lengths but continuing the plainspoken folk style of her earlier records. It functions as a between-albums release rather than a major statement. Best for listeners already following her catalog.
lineage: A minor release bridging 'Miss River' and her later, more produced work.

label: Self-released
description: Recorded live at Louisiana's Dockside Studio and self-produced, this album leans harder into vintage New Orleans R&B and Cajun two-step rhythms than her earlier folk-leaning records, fronted by her full electric band. It's a looser, more rhythmic record built for dancing, paying homage to Fats Domino and Irma Thomas as much as to folk songwriting. Good for listeners who want Quintana's most fully-arranged, band-forward work.
lineage: Quintana's most recent album, continuing her run of self-released, New Orleans-rooted records.

album: That's All There Is (And There Ain't No More)
label: Muddy Roots Records
description: A hard-country record steeped in honky-tonk shuffles and blue-collar songwriting, cut by a band that formed busking on New Orleans streets before relocating. It's twangier and more traditionalist than the Deslondes' genre-blending, closer to classic Bakersfield/outlaw phrasing than to R&B. The band and Reedy's songwriting are cited as a direct influence on the Deslondes' street-country sound.
lineage: Formed in New Orleans' street-country scene that also produced the Deslondes, who have named Reedy as an influence.

label: Self-released
description: A long-gestating follow-up built around travel and homesickness, keeping the band's classic honky-tonk instrumentation of twangy electric guitar and pedal steel over Reedy's plainspoken, working-class songwriting. It's a more matured, settled record than the band's earlier, rowdier output. For fans of traditionalist country songwriting with a road-worn edge.
lineage: Reedy relocated from New Orleans to Chicago between records, but the band's sound and origin remain tied to the New Orleans street-country scene that shaped the Deslondes.

album: The Place That You Call Home
label: Parish Road Music
description: The debut album by New Orleans songwriter Kelcy Mae Wilburn under the band name Ever More Nest, an Americana record centered on the idea of place and rootedness, from Mississippi trees to Louisiana home. It pairs a plainspoken, weathered alto with pedal steel and understated full-band arrangements, closer to alt-country balladry than to the city's brass-and-R&B side. It was nominated for Best Alt-Country Album at the Independent Music Awards.
lineage: Part of the same 2010s New Orleans Americana scene that produced Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes.

label: Bayou Perdu Records
description: A Grammy-nominated Cajun record that runs traditional two-step fiddle and French-language singing through distortion pedals and rock-band volume, closer to a noisy roots-punk gig than a dancehall set. It's trad-Cajun instrumentation (fiddle, accordion) pushed into feedback and fuzz. It's for listeners exploring how far a traditional Louisiana form can be pushed toward rock.
lineage: Sits in the trad-Cajun/newgrass Context lane rather than the Deslondes/Riff Raff alt-country lineage, but shares the same New Orleans-area roots-music community and stages; the split is genre (trad Cajun vs. country-rock songwriting) rather than geography.

label: Rice Pump Records
description: A Grammy-winning Cajun record that folds synthesizers and studio effects into traditional fiddle-and-accordion two-steps, continuing the band's project of modernizing Cajun music without abandoning its French-language core. It's denser and more electronic than 'Mammoth Waltz', while keeping the same two-step dance rhythms. For listeners wanting the trad-Cajun wing of the wider Louisiana roots scene.
lineage: Same trad-Cajun lineage as 'Mammoth Waltz'; connected to the broader New Orleans-area Americana community by geography and shared festival stages, not by songwriting style.

label: Crafted Sounds
description: Life on the Lawn is a Philadelphia four-piece's plodding, guitar-forward indie rock record, closing on the loping, anxious 'Wasting the Weekends.' The songs move at a deliberate, unhurried pace that a reviewer likened to slowcore, wrapped around conversational, downcast lyrics. It sits closer to the scene's slacker and power-pop wing than to overt country, but the tempo and mood put it in dialogue with the Core's quieter side.
lineage: Grows out of 2010s indie/slacker rock in the vein of Pavement-descended bands, with a slowcore undertow that connects it to the Core's hushed-twang lane.

label: cooked raw
description: Recorded and written entirely during 2020 quarantine, this self-titled debut is a spare, home-recorded set of guitar rock from Philadelphia duo Garrett and Derek. The songs are short and plainly played, favoring direct, diary-like lyrics over polish, and it was later reissued by Crafted Sounds in 2023 once the band's following grew.
lineage: A DIY, pandemic-era continuation of the Bandcamp slacker-rock tradition that the band would later sharpen on Life on the Lawn.

label: Self-released
description: Spent is a ten-song set of plainspoken, guitar-driven folk-rock from St. John's songwriter Andrew Smith, tagged by the artist himself as folk and alt-country. The songs are built from long, narrative verses about touring, fading friendships, and small-town memory, sung in a conversational near-talk-sing delivery. It was also pressed to vinyl, suggesting a committed local following for the project.
lineage: Continues the plainspoken, guitar-and-voice songwriting line that runs from '90s alt-country through 2010s Bandcamp singer-songwriters.

label: Self-released
description: Glutton For Punishment is Kansas City band Big Fat Cow's fuzzed-out country-rock record, self-tagged 'fuzz folk' and 'post rock' alongside 'country' and 'folk.' A song called 'Goodbye Gram Parsons' makes the band's cosmic-country reference points explicit, while the rest of the record piles distorted guitar onto loose, rootsy song structures. It is the rowdier, longer of the band's two Core-era full releases.
lineage: Draws a direct line from Gram Parsons-style cosmic country through fuzzed-up 2010s-2020s indie-twang bands.

label: Self-released
description: A five-song follow-up EP that opens with 'Yellow Belly Boy' and keeps Big Fat Cow's fuzzy, country-tagged guitar rock intact in a shorter format. The band again tags itself 'fuzz folk' and 'post rock' alongside straight 'country,' and the songs keep the loose, rowdy energy of their full-length in a tighter run of tracks.
lineage: A shorter continuation of the band's cosmic-country/fuzz-folk sound established on Glutton For Punishment.

label: Self-released
description: Good Grief is Birmingham, Alabama band Bitter Calm's debut full-length, self-tagged 'chamber rock' and 'slowcore.' The eight songs move at a hushed, unhurried pace with sparse arrangements built around clean guitar and restrained vocals, matching the band's own description of itself as 'big big sad.' It is the quieter, earlier half of the band's Core-era catalog.
lineage: Sits in the Low/Duster-descended slowcore-and-sadcore line, rendered by a young indie band rather than a '90s one.

album: Eternity In The Lake of Fire
label: Self-released
description: Eternity In The Lake of Fire is Bitter Calm's nine-song second record, again tagged 'chamber rock,' 'indie rock,' and 'slowcore' on the band's own page. The band's liner notes describe it as a record about 'self-annihilation' and 'accepting one's own hopelessness,' fronted by singer/guitarist Michael Harp with violin, bass, and percussion support from Birmingham musicians. Includes 'Sinner,' the playlist's entry point to the band.
lineage: Extends the slowcore, sadness-as-method tradition into a darker, more full-band-oriented record than the debut.

label: Self-released
description: There Will Be Chicken Wings is a twelve-song Raleigh, North Carolina record self-tagged 'southern rock,' 'alt country,' 'countrycore,' and 'countrygaze' on Bandcamp, and produced by Colin Miller (himself a figure in this scene). It moves between rowdy, full-band roots rock and slower, heavier passages, with plainspoken lyrics about small-town Southern life. Bandcamp fans who bought it also collected Wednesday's catalog, underlining its place in the same wall-of-guitar country lineage.
lineage: Follows the Wednesday-style template of loud, distorted guitars under country song structure that defines the countrygaze lane.

label: Self-released
description: Sunfall is an Austin songwriter's ten-track home-recorded record, self-tagged 'americana,' 'california country,' and 'psychedelic folk.' The songs are warm and unhurried, built on acoustic fingerpicking and drifting, sun-bleached melodies rather than twang or fiddle. It plays like a bedroom-scale entry in the Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic-country revival.
lineage: Channels the breezy, Gram Parsons/Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic-country sound through a solo, DIY bedroom recording.

label: Self-released
description: A seven-song companion EP from the same year as Sunfall, tagged with the same 'americana,' 'folk-psych,' and 'psychedelic' terms. It keeps the same hazy, acoustic-led sound in a shorter run of songs. The playlist's 'Trickshot' is a later standalone single by the same artist, not on this release.
lineage: A shorter, same-year sibling to Sunfall in Buckley Willis's cosmic-country/psych-folk catalog.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: Famous Lunch is New Orleans songwriter Chris Acker's tenth-song fourth full-length, tagged 'alt country,' 'americana,' and 'country folk' by the artist. Backed by his Growing Boys bandmates (including pedal steel from Nikolai Shveitser), Acker sings plainspoken, funny-then-heartbreaking narrative songs recorded live in the room. Includes 'Wouldn't Do For You (Buddy),' the playlist's pick and one of the record's centerpieces.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Prine/Townes-descended plainspoken storytelling line, filtered through a working New Orleans dancehall band.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: Odd, Ordinary, & Otherwise is Chris Acker's thirteen-song third full-length, again tagged 'alt country,' 'americana,' and 'country folk.' The Bandcamp liner notes describe it as ranging from 'introspective, quiet tunes' to 'downright barn burners,' written partly during 2020 isolation. It shows the same plainspoken, detail-heavy songwriting that runs through his catalog.
lineage: Part of the same New Orleans folk-and-dancehall songwriting practice that produced Famous Lunch three years later.

label: Self-released
description: Slow Country is a twelve-song record from Chicago's Conor Lynch, self-tagged 'folk rock,' 'indie rock,' and 'singer-songwriter' with a self-described 'mid-fi' aesthetic. Song titles like 'Steam Whistle' and 'Long Ways From Home' point to the record's rural, travel-worn imagery, set over loose, unpolished guitar arrangements. The playlist's two tracks come from a separate 2025 single rather than this album.
lineage: A lo-fi, home-recorded take on folk-rock storytelling in the Bandcamp singer-songwriter tradition.

label: Self-released
description: Cooper Kenward's self-titled twelve-song debut is tagged 'alternative,' 'folk,' and 'singer-songwriter' by the Los Angeles artist. The songs favor plain, conversational lyrics over polish, in the vein of the barroom and bedroom-folk wing of the Core scene. It predates the artist's move to a proper label for his next two records.
lineage: Early, DIY-scale entry in the same LA singer-songwriter lane later refined on Dying in a Diner.

label: Soggy Anvil Records
description: Dying in a Diner is Cooper Kenward's ten-song Soggy Anvil Records release, still tagged 'alternative,' 'folk,' and 'singer-songwriter.' The artist's own liner notes describe the record as being about memory, 'like looking through an album of old photos,' with songs that range from loose and unguarded to slow-built. 'Wheelies,' the track that led the playlist here, appears on Kenward's next record rather than this one.
lineage: Continues the plainspoken LA singer-songwriter thread that later drew comparisons in the Americana press to MJ Lenderman-adjacent songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: Always The Moon is a nine-song Pensacola, Florida record self-tagged 'folk,' 'country,' and 'indie.' The songs are guitar-and-voice driven, with plainspoken, downcast titles ('Father Time,' 'Treading Water,' 'Sycophant To Sorrow') typical of the singer-songwriter side of the scene. The playlist's 'World Series' comes from a later 2025 EP too short to qualify on its own, but confirms the same artist and sound.
lineage: A small-scale, self-released entry in the plainspoken new-country/singer-songwriter lane.

label: Self-released
description: sending is a six-song EP from Harrisonburg, Virginia band Dogwood Tales, mixed and mastered by Danny Gibney. It includes an early version of 'mt jackson,' a song about the songwriter's uncle's hospitalization that the band would later re-record for a full-length. The EP's tone is plainspoken and small-town-focused, consistent with the rest of the band's catalog.
lineage: An early sketch of songs the band would develop further on Every Star in Rockingham County.

label: WarHen Records
description: Rodeo is a six-song vinyl EP (catalog WH066) credited to a full band lineup of acoustic and electric guitar, bass, pedal steel (Stephen Kuester), and drums, engineered by Erik Romero in Ocean, NJ. It is a straightforward alt-country record built on real pedal steel and full-band arrangements rather than fuzz or distortion.
lineage: Represents the more traditionally country-instrumented side of Dogwood Tales' catalog, released through the same regional vinyl label as 13 Summers 13 Falls.

label: WarHen Records
description: 13 Summers 13 Falls is a five-song vinyl EP (catalog WH065) released the same year as Rodeo through WarHen Records. It keeps the band's plainspoken, small-town songwriting in a shorter, quieter set than its companion release.
lineage: A same-year, same-label companion to Rodeo in Dogwood Tales' developing alt-country catalog.

label: Born Losers Records
description: Every Star in Rockingham County is Dogwood Tales' twelve-song Born Losers Records full-length, fronted by childhood friends Kyle Grim and Ben Ryan. The label copy describes pedal steel chords, delicate harmonization, and 'jamming power pop drumlines' set against lyrics about small-town Shenandoah Valley life, hospital bills, and pop-culture touchstones like Princess Peach and McDonald's. It re-records 'Mt. Jackson,' the EP-era song about the songwriter's hospitalized uncle, as its emotional centerpiece.
lineage: Explicitly framed by its own label copy as continuing the Townes Van Zandt-descended songwriting tradition inside 'indie rock's current Lo-Fi country romanticism.'

label: Self-released
description: Fat, Evil Children's self-titled six-song EP is tagged 'americana,' 'indie folk,' and 'indie rock' by the Los Angeles band. It includes 'Weedpuller,' the playlist's entry point, alongside plainspoken, mid-tempo songs that lean folk and Americana rather than punk or fuzz despite the band's name.
lineage: A small-scale LA entry in the 2010s-2020s Bandcamp Americana/indie-folk lane.

label: Self-released
description: Can't Stop is Fat, Evil Children's second six-song EP, tagged with the addition of 'emo' alongside the band's usual 'americana' and 'indie folk' tags. The songs keep the same plainspoken, mid-tempo approach as the debut EP, with slightly more emotionally direct, anthemic moments.
lineage: A continuation of the band's Americana/indie-folk sound with a newly added emo edge, connecting it to the scene's emo-twang crossover wing.

label: Meritorio Records
description: swan is New Zealand songwriter Peter McCall's second full-length as Fazed on a Pony, tagged 'alt-country,' 'emo,' and 'indie rock.' The label copy says it expands from the project's earlier 'Pavement-esque tuneful indie rock' into arrangements with pedal steel, fiddle, drum machines, and synths, and explicitly cites comparisons to MJ Lenderman, David Berman, and Sparklehorse. Includes 'Heart Goes Blank,' the playlist's pick.
lineage: Its own label copy places it in the Lenderman/Berman/Sparklehorse lineage of wry, twangy indie songwriting, translated into an 'antipodean' idiom.

label: Self-released
description: it'll all work out is Fazed on a Pony's earlier eight-song full-length, tagged 'alt-country,' 'emo,' and 'indie rock' like its follow-up. It represents the more straightforwardly 'Pavement-esque' indie-rock sound that swan's own liner notes say the project later expanded outward from.
lineage: The earlier, leaner version of the alt-country/indie-rock songwriting Fazed on a Pony built out further on swan.

label: Self-released
description: Chicago quartet's debut EP mixes big fuzzed-out guitar riffs with twangy pedal steel, mandolin and bass harmonica, self-recorded live at the band's practice space in summer 2023. The four songs move from house-show stomp to honky-tonk shuffle, with Nathan Zurawski's abstract, personal lyrics giving the psychedelic country-rock an introspective edge. It plays like a scrappy, DIY-recorded take on 60s/70s country-rock filtered through an indie band's practice-space budget.
lineage: Self-described as a 'Country and Folk, Power Pop and Rock n' Roll' band drawing on 60s-70s country production, in line with the pedal-steel-and-fuzz indie-twang scene.

label: Ghost Ramp Records
description: GracieHorse's early full-length is billed on Bandcamp under alt-country and 'bummer jams' tags, a Los Angeles songwriter working a direct, unguarded confessional style over rock-leaning arrangements. Tracks like 'Youth is a Fire' and 'Tightrope' pair plainspoken, heartbreak-adjacent lyrics with a loose, road-worn band sound. It is the record that established the storytelling, no-frills approach she carried into her later work.
lineage: Early work from an LA singer-songwriter who Bandcamp files under alt-country/rock, predating her more overtly country-soul later releases.

label: Self-released
description: Idle County bill themselves as 'WNC farm-rock' out of Asheville, and their debut LP is tagged country, alt-country and rock n roll on Bandcamp. Song titles like 'Lebanon, TN' and 'Sin City' point to travelogue, small-town storytelling over a straightforward country-rock band sound. A Facebook review of the album compares it directly to 'prime late-90s alt-country,' which lines up with the plainspoken, guitar-forward feel of the tracklist.
lineage: Rooted in the 90s alt-country sound (Wilco/Uncle Tupelo-adjacent) as filtered through the 2020s Asheville scene.

label: Self-released
description: Jacob Tremont's ten-song junebug is tagged countrygaze alongside folk, acoustic pop and lo-fi indie-folk on Bandcamp, a bedroom-recorded singer-songwriter set built around fingerpicked guitar and plainspoken lyrics. Song titles ('garden,' 'diner,' 'steamboat') suggest small, quiet vignettes rather than big statements, thanked in the liner notes to friends across several New Jersey towns and Philadelphia. It's an intimate, home-recorded record that leans on the hushed, countrygaze-tagged end of DIY singer-songwriter music.
lineage: Self-tagged 'countrygaze,' placing it alongside the hushed, DIY singer-songwriter wing of the current indie-folk/twang scene.

label: Self-released
description: A six-song follow-up to junebug, carrying the same countrygaze/lo-fi indie-folk tags on Bandcamp. Tracks like 'no, i'm not afraid' and 'seven years of bad luck' continue the plainspoken, home-recorded singer-songwriter approach in shorter form. It reads as a between-albums EP rather than a full statement.
lineage: Continuation of the countrygaze-tagged, DIY bedroom-folk sound of junebug.

label: Self-released
description: Billed a 'New York songman,' Josh Bolin's four-song debut EP is tagged cosmic americana alongside folk and indie rock on Bandcamp. The songs favor warm, unhurried arrangements over acoustic-and-electric guitar interplay, in keeping with the cosmic-country lineage of buttery lead guitar and easy tempos. It's a compact introduction rather than a full statement.
lineage: Tagged 'cosmic americana' by the artist, tying it to the Gram Parsons/Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic country revival.

label: Self-released
description: Recorded live to a thrift-store cassette recorder in a cabin in Killbuck, Ohio, this Canton, Ohio band's debut is tagged Americana, classic rock and garage rock on Bandcamp. Its own liner notes describe a 'son-rock' aesthetic of 'heartland-soaked tunes full of Americana angst and Rust Belt blues,' including 'On the Road Again, Again,' described as 'a truck-driver's zen-like meditations set to the loop of a Willie Nelson tape.' It's raspy, tape-hiss Midwestern rock about family friction and dead-end towns.
lineage: Self-described 'son-rock' in the heartland/Rust Belt Americana vein, cabin-recorded on cassette.

album: Blue heeler in ugly snowlight, grey on gray on gray on white.
label: Self-released
description: James Keegan's solo bedroom-pop project Kitchen released this sprawling 20-track album from Rochester, New York, home-recorded and plainly designed. Songs like 'Real Estate Agent' pair conversational, self-lacerating lyrics ('I always try to keep it light / unless I'm drunk on a Saturday night') with spare, lo-fi arrangements. It's DIY slacker songwriting rather than country per se, closer to the bedroom end of the Bandcamp indie-rock scene than to twang.
lineage: A solo lo-fi/DIY bedroom-indie project without an explicit country lineage; included here for its conversational, home-recorded slacker songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: Local Superstar's self-titled album is tagged indie rock, alt-country and folk rock on Bandcamp and was recorded at Drop of Sun Studios in Asheville, NC. Song titles like 'Passing By Waco,' 'Dog Song' and 'Drinkin' to Write' point to loose, road- and drinking-song-flavored guitar rock. It's an eight-song set from a Savannah, Georgia project working the same alt-country-leaning indie-rock lane as its Asheville recording home.
lineage: Recorded at Drop of Sun Studios (Asheville), a hub for the current alt-country-adjacent indie scene.

label: Self-released
description: Lowell Thompson's ten-song Stranger's Advice is tagged rock, alt-country and 'vermont' on Bandcamp (the artist's page also carries an Austin, TX tag, suggesting some relocation between the two). Songs like 'Bradley Street' and 'Meadow Lane' point toward plainspoken, place-named storytelling over straightforward alt-country arrangements. It's a 2014 full-length that predates his later duo work as Lowell Thompson & Crown Pilot.
lineage: Vermont/Austin-tagged alt-country singer-songwriter work, part of the same 2010s wave of indie-scene country songwriters.

label: Self-released
description: Wellington, New Zealand's Mudgoose tags this ten-song album lofi folk, outsider folk, loner folk and experimental folk on Bandcamp. 'Mary's Lost' features vocalist Mieke (per the artist's Instagram) over the hushed, homemade arrangements typical of the record. It's quiet, DIY loner-folk rather than country, closer to the lo-fi/outsider end of the current Bandcamp singer-songwriter underground.
lineage: Self-tagged loner/outsider lo-fi folk, part of the DIY Bandcamp network rather than a country lineage.

label: New Rose
description: Los Angeles band New Rose's eleven-song Morning Haze is tagged 'country' on Bandcamp, with a tracklist ('Country Noise,' 'Should've Been A Wedding,' 'Pearl Buttons') that reads as a set of plainspoken country-rock songs about heartbreak and small betrayals. 'Should've Been A Wedding' recurs on the band's earlier All Nite EP as well, suggesting it was a live favorite carried into the full-length. It's a straightforward, guitar-and-twang alt-country record from an LA band.
lineage: Self-tagged 'country,' part of the current alt-country-leaning West Coast indie scene.

label: Self-released
description: Washington, DC's Heaven Forbid bill themselves 'High Faultin' Rootin' Tootin' Sons of Guns,' and their eight-song debut album is a straightforward honky-tonk record, per the band's own Bandcamp copy: '8 new favorites and country classics in high fidelity.' 'Lonesome DC Cowboy' (on the band's earlier Three Songs EP) is explicitly based on Peter Rowan's 'Lonesome LA Cowboy,' underlining the band's classic-honky-tonk frame of reference. A Washington City Paper feature described the band as 'bringing the punk ethos to country music.'
lineage: Punk-scene musicians playing straight honky-tonk/classic country, per Washington City Paper's description of the band's punk-to-country crossover.

label: Self-released
description: Alabama songwriter Jameson Hubbard's debut album under the name Haysop was tracked at Taylor Hollingsworth's Birmingham home studio with pedal steel guitarist Conor Rector and singer-songwriter Janet Simpson guesting. The Bandcamp liner notes call the record 'a rock 'n' roll album through and through,' pairing Muscle Shoals-indebted guitar and Wurlitzer with Hubbard's Kurt Vile-esque, deadpan-tinged songwriting about a 'budding relationship.' It's a 13-song set that swings from full-throttle rockers to loose front-porch picking.
lineage: Built from an Alabama bar-band and blues-scene background (SQQUAT, Alabama Blues Project) into a Muscle Shoals-recorded country-rock debut.

label: Self-released
description: A five-song debut EP from a Jackson, Mississippi band that pairs pedal steel with fuzzed-out, loosely played guitar rock. The band's own Bandcamp tags it alongside twangcore and countrygaze, and songs like "Built to Rust" and "Nebraska" lean into ragged, mid-tempo indie-twang. It plays like a rougher-edged cousin to the Wednesday/MJ Lenderman school of loud guitar country.
lineage: Grows out of the 2010s-2020s countrygaze/indie-twang wave (Wednesday, MJ Lenderman) that puts pedal steel inside noisy indie rock guitars.

label: Self-released
description: A follow-up five-song EP from Rose Haven Motor Hotel, tagged on Bandcamp as country-alt, indie folk and indie rock. It closes with "Just Fine, Thanks," a quieter, more resigned song than the debut EP's rowdier moments, suggesting a band moving between loud indie-twang and hushed indie folk within the same short release.
lineage: Continues the band's countrygaze/indie-twang lane established on their debut EP.

label: Self-released
description: A four-song EP from this Nashville band, whose Bandcamp bio promises "Rocking & Rolling & Twanging & Banging" and tags itself twang rock and alt-country. Ringing, jangly guitars sit over straightforward rock rhythm section, closer to loose bar-band indie-twang than polished Americana.
lineage: Part of the 2010s-2020s Nashville DIY scene folding twang and jangle into indie rock songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: A four-song live recording taped in Allston, Massachusetts, tagged twang rock and alt-country on the band's Bandcamp. It captures Save Henry's ringing, jangly guitar approach in a bar-show setting rather than the studio.
lineage: Documents the same Nashville twang-rock project in a live setting.

label: bugsounds
description: A ten-song Philadelphia record self-tagged on Bandcamp as Americana, alt-country, art rock and emo at once. "Michigan" and the rest of the album move between twangy indie rock and more anxious, emo-inflected structures, putting it close to the emo-twang crossover strand of the current scene.
lineage: Fits the emo-and-DIY-punk-into-twang line that also produced bands like Truth Club and MJ Lenderman's peers.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song debut album from Toronto's Matt Jonn Lewis, written as a tribute to his late brother Josh; the Bandcamp tags run alt-country, indie folk and lo-fi. Songs like "hank, paint & country star" wear their country-folk debt openly inside plain, home-recorded arrangements.
lineage: Sits in the lo-fi/indie-folk end of the 2010s Bandcamp twang scene, closer to home-taped folk than loud guitar rock.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song follow-up tagged alt-country, bedroom pop, indie folk and lo-fi on Bandcamp. It keeps Spirit Josh's plainspoken, home-recorded style, moving between quiet folk arrangements and slightly fuller indie-pop structures across songs like "Hotel Motel" and "Terminal Love."
lineage: Continues the same lo-fi indie-folk-into-alt-country project as the 2019 debut.

label: Self-released
description: An eight-song album tagged alt-country and indie folk, closing with "Staying Up & Drinkin' Wine." Song titles like "Straight Outta Dodge" and "Trout! Fishing!" keep the wry, plainspoken tone of Spirit Josh's earlier records inside a slightly more full-band arrangement.
lineage: Third album in the same Toronto lo-fi/alt-country project.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song Chicago record the band tags on Bandcamp as Americana, alt-country, country punk and cowpunk all at once. Songs like "Funeral Home" and "Gas" move at a fast, punky clip with twangy guitar leads, putting it squarely in the punk-kids-play-country tradition.
lineage: Direct descendant of cowpunk (X, Jason & the Scorchers) filtered through 2010s-2020s DIY indie-rock recording.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song self-titled record, again tagged alt-country, country punk and cowpunk by the band. "Eggs" and "Drunk at the Airport" keep the same fast, twangy cowpunk attack as the earlier record, with titles that lean into deadpan, everyday absurdity.
lineage: A later entry in St. Marlboro's cowpunk/alt-country catalog.

label: Teal Peel
description: A nine-song debut album credited with a dedicated pedal steel player (Landon Gay) on Bandcamp, built around what the band calls a "dynamic and improvisational" live style. "Sandy" and the rest of Country River lean breezy and jam-friendly rather than raw or fast, closer to the cosmic-country/70s-revival end of the current scene than to punk-adjacent twang.
lineage: Follows the Dead/Gram Parsons-descended cosmic-country revival of buttery lead guitar and pedal steel over relaxed tempos.

label: Self-released
description: The debut LP from this self-described "alt-country quintet" out of Nashville, a nine-song set that includes "Weatherman." The band's own copy calls it the product of "several years' worth of work," and the Bandcamp tags (Americana, alt-country, folk punk) place it as a full-band, recognizably country-structured record rather than a noisier indie-twang one.
lineage: A straightforward continuation of 2010s-2020s alt-country bands playing recognizable country structures with indie-scene provenance.

album: The Reverend Earl Dogwood and His Downstreamers
label: Self-released
description: The band's first EP, four songs tagged acoustic, americana, classic country and country rock on Bandcamp. It is a more stripped-down, acoustic-leaning start for a band that would fill out into a full alt-country quintet on their debut LP.
lineage: Founding release of The Downstreamers' Nashville alt-country project.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song record from Wyatt Dronen's solo project, tagged countrygaze and lofi country on Bandcamp. "Falling" and "Keep True" sit among plainspoken, lo-fi arrangements; the band's own bio describes the songwriting as queer love songs leaning into limerence, set to alt-country and indie guitar.
lineage: Part of the lo-fi/countrygaze wing of the current indie-twang scene, closer to bedroom recording than full-band rock.

label: Self-released
description: An earlier ten-song Walker Rider record, tagged alternative country and lofi country. Songs such as "North Country" and the title track keep the same hushed, home-recorded alt-country approach as the later Fair, with a title track that leans directly into cowboy-song imagery.
lineage: Earlier entry in Walker Rider's lo-fi alt-country catalog.

label: twosyllable records
description: A ten-song folk record released on twosyllable records, tagged simply "folk" on Bandcamp. "Berry on a Briar" and songs like "Sheep Guts" and "Letting Go" are quiet, fingerpicked and plainspoken, closer to hushed indie folk than twangy rock.
lineage: Sits in the folk-songwriting line running from Townes/Gillian Welch through the 2010s Bandcamp scene.

album: My Love Is Occupational and There's Nothing I'd Rather Do
label: Self-released
description: A ten-song Charlottesville record the band's own bio describes as pulling from "regional forebears Sparklehorse and Dave Berman": "shoegaze with eye contact, country without the cowboy hat." The Bandcamp tags (alternative, indie, slacker, soft rock) fit a slack, mid-tempo indie-rock record with a country undertow rather than an overt twang band.
lineage: Follows the Sparklehorse/Silver Jews line of soft, slack indie rock with a country undertow, feeding into the current slacker/jangle revival.

label: Born Losers Records
description: A ten-song Brooklyn record on Born Losers Records; the band's own copy frames it as a folk-rock project in the Liz Phair/Jenny Lewis mold, equal parts polished pop songwriting and loose band-practice energy. "Big Parking Lot" and the rest keep a wry, conversational tone over jangly, mid-fi guitar pop.
lineage: Sits in the 2010s-2020s guitar-pop revival descended from jangle and slacker indie rock, with a wink toward '90s alt-rock songwriters like Liz Phair.

label: Self-released
description: A ten-song debut LP from this Asheville band, whose Bandcamp tags run alt-country, noise rock, shoegaze and slowcore together. The band describes it as the product of years spent writing through depression, substance abuse and disassociation, and the songs move slowly and heavily, with country structure buried under guitar noise.
lineage: Builds on the countrygaze template (Wednesday) of shoegaze-scale guitar walls under country song structure.

album: How Could I Be So In Debt?
label: Self-released
description: A second ten-song LP tagged the same way as the debut (alt-country, noise rock, shoegaze, slowcore); a local Asheville-music roundup described it as shoegaze meeting country, with steel guitar meshing into the band's dense, slow-building arrangements. A 2025 single, "Bear Down," followed this album but was not gathered onto either LP.
lineage: Second full-length in Tombstone Poetry's countrygaze/slowcore catalog.
key_tracks: How Could I Be So In Debt?

label: PNKSLM Recordings
description: An eight-song debut LP on PNKSLM Recordings, tagged alternative and alt-country on Bandcamp. Bandleader Ben Hambro's songwriting is dryly funny and plainspoken, closer to talk-sung indie-country than polished Americana.
lineage: Part of the UK's small alt-country/indie-twang scene, distinct from the mostly American Core wave.

album: long time caller, first time listener
label: PNKSLM Recordings
description: A nine-song second LP on PNKSLM, compiling and following up the band's earlier long time caller and first time listener releases; the band's own copy frames it around Ben Hambro's dryly funny songwriting and the real sadness underneath it. The track birkenstocks and other pop-culture-referencing titles keep the same dry, talk-sung alt-country tone.
lineage: Second full-length from vegas water taxi's London alt-country project.

label: Self-released
description: An eleven-song debut album the band describes on its own Bandcamp page as modern DIY indie alt-country, with an earnest, twangy vocal delivery and a hint of distortion behind nimble guitar lines. "Frontyard" and the rest of the record match that description closely, and Bandcamp tags it country alongside indie, rock and acoustic.
lineage: A clear example of punk/indie-raised musicians playing directly toward alt-country structure and twang.

label: Self-released
description: A fourteen-song second album, tagged rock, acoustic, indie and pop on Bandcamp. It keeps the same twang-inflected, DIY indie-rock approach as the debut, with a title track that appears in both a "loud" and a "quiet" version bookending the record.
lineage: Second full-length from hey i'm outside's alt-country project.
